hints: Convert the given wavelength $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ to nanometres to compare with familiar spectrum values.
Recall that visible light is roughly $400 \text{ nm}$ to $700 \text{ nm}$, so check whether $100 \text{ nm}$ is longer or shorter than violet light.
Recall the order of decreasing wavelength around visible light: infra-red, visible, ultraviolet, then X-ray.
walkthrough: Identify the given value: wavelength $\lambda = 1.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.
Convert to nanometres: $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 100 \text{ nm}$ since $1 \text{ nm} = 10^{-9} \text{ m}$.
Recall approximate ranges: visible is about $400-700 \text{ nm}$, infra-red is longer than red at $>700 \text{ nm}$, ultraviolet is shorter than violet at about $10-400 \text{ nm}$.
Compare $100 \text{ nm}$ with these ranges: it is shorter than visible but longer than typical X-rays of less than about $10 \text{ nm}$.
Therefore the $100 \text{ nm}$ wave fits the ultraviolet region. This is option B.

options.A: Infra-red has much longer wavelength than $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, typically about $10^{-6} \text{ m}$ to $10^{-3} \text{ m}$.
options.B: A wavelength of $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ or $100 \text{ nm}$ lies just shorter than visible light, in the ultraviolet region.
options.C: Visible light is about $4 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ to $7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, so $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ is too short to be visible.
options.D: X-rays have still shorter wavelengths, typically $10^{-11} \text{ m}$ to $10^{-8} \text{ m}$, so $10^{-7} \text{ m}$ is too long.
